# Undernutrition & malnutrition

> *Malnutrition can be present at a normal or even high BMI, so it is rarely noticed unless someone
> screens for it, and in Singapore it is often missed among frail, isolated and hospitalised older
> adults. We cover what malnutrition does to the body, how to recognise and screen for it, oral nutrition
> support and texture-modified food, and when to refer.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how a deficit of energy, protein or micronutrients leads, through loss of muscle, to weakness,
  poor healing and higher mortality.
- Distinguish starvation-related, chronic disease-related and acute disease- or injury-related
  malnutrition by their degree of inflammation, and explain why disease-related malnutrition resists
  feeding alone.
- Explain why a normal or high BMI excludes neither malnutrition nor sarcopenia.
- Identify the patients to screen, and interpret a positive MUST screen as a risk flag that triggers
  referral, not a diagnosis.
- Describe the stepwise approach to oral nutrition support, from food-first through food fortification to
  oral nutritional supplements.
- Recognise refeeding risk and the red flags of dysphagia, and refer.
:::

## Undernutrition & malnutrition at a glance {#sec-overview}

In its broad sense, malnutrition covers both overnutrition and **undernutrition**. Undernutrition is the
deficit form, and it is what clinical screening and diagnosis mean by **malnutrition**. In that sense
malnutrition is a disease state: a deficit of energy, protein or micronutrients that measurably changes body composition and
function and worsens outcomes. The frail, undernourished senior is as much a nutritional patient as the
person with metabolic syndrome (see the *Obesity & metabolic syndrome* chapter). Healthy ageing is ageing
*in health* (see the *Healthy ageing* chapter); malnutrition is the pathological state that ageing, illness
and isolation tip people into.

Three principles shape the clinical approach to malnutrition:

- Malnutrition is a diagnosable disease, so it should be screened for before it looks obvious. It is common in the community as well as on the ward, and it is routinely missed [@cederholm2017espenTerminology; @wei2017slasFrailty].
- A normal or high BMI does not exclude it. Weight loss and acute illness harm nutrition independently of body size, and a person can be losing muscle at a healthy weight [@bapenMUST; @cruzjentoft2019ewgsop2].
- The generalist's job is to suspect, screen and refer. Screening flags risk and triggers referral; the assessment, diagnosis and feeding plan are led by the dietitian and the team [@jensen2019glim; @aclm2022comp].

## Pathophysiology: what malnutrition does to the body {#sec-mal-science}

Malnutrition is defined by a causal chain, not by body size, and that chain is what makes a wasted, weak
patient a medical problem. A deficit of energy, protein or micronutrients produces a measurable change in
body composition: a loss of fat and, above all, of muscle. That loss in turn causes functional and clinical
harm: weakness, falls, poor wound healing, more infections, longer hospital stays and higher mortality
[@cederholm2017espenTerminology]. A sustained deficit draws its protein from muscle, which is working
tissue, not a designed store (see the fasted and starved states in the
[*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-starvation) chapter, and body composition in the
*Energy balance* chapter).

![Malnutrition is a causal chain, not a body size. A deficit of energy and protein, worsened by disease-driven inflammation and reduced intake, produces loss of fat and especially of muscle, which causes weakness, poor healing, infection, longer stays and higher mortality. The three aetiological categories sit on an inflammation gradient, from starvation-related (no inflammation) through chronic disease-related (mild to moderate) to acute disease- or injury-related (severe). Inflammation is why disease-related malnutrition resists feeding alone.](/figures/mechanisms/malnutrition-mechanism.svg){#fig-malnutrition width="92%" fig-align="center"}

Inflammation is the basis of the classification by cause, and it explains why some malnutrition responds
poorly to feeding alone. Three types are distinguished by how much inflammation is present
[@jensen2010etiologyMalnutrition; @cederholm2017espenTerminology]:

Starvation-related malnutrition
: Malnutrition from a pure intake deficit, without inflammation.

Chronic disease-related malnutrition
: Malnutrition with mild-to-moderate inflammation, as in heart failure, cancer or kidney disease; also
  called cachexia (illness-driven wasting of muscle, often with loss of fat).

Acute disease- or injury-related malnutrition
: Malnutrition with severe inflammation, as in acute illness or injury.

Inflammation drives catabolism and blunts appetite (for how appetite is regulated, see the *Appetite and
weight regulation* chapter). **Disease-related malnutrition**, the chronic and acute types together,
therefore resists feeding alone: extra feeding cannot simply outpace inflammation-driven catabolism, and
the underlying disease has to be treated too.

::: {.example}
Roughly 46% of patients with heart failure are malnourished, and malnutrition about doubles their
mortality [@lv2021hfMalnutrition].
:::

Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle strength and mass (see the *Healthy ageing* chapter), is a
muscle disorder, diagnosed on low strength confirmed by low muscle quantity, and is related to but distinct
from a nutritional deficit [@cruzjentoft2019ewgsop2]. The two overlap: reduced muscle mass is a feature of
malnutrition, and a nutritional deficit accelerates muscle loss. However, a person can be sarcopenic at a
normal or high BMI; with obesity, the combination is **sarcopenic obesity**. Muscle therefore has to be
assessed as well as weight.

In Singapore the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS 2019) cut-offs apply, because European values
overestimate the deficit in smaller-framed populations [@chen2020awgs2019; @limSarcopeniaCpg2022]. The
muscle–bone overlap, and the resistance-exercise and bone-loading side of protecting the frail patient, are
in the *Bone & joint health* chapter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a malnourished patient with heart failure is offered plenty of food. Why is feeding alone unlikely to reverse the malnutrition?
Heart failure is a chronic disease with mild-to-moderate inflammation, so this is disease-related
malnutrition. Inflammation drives catabolism and blunts appetite, so extra food cannot simply outpace the
inflammation-driven catabolism; the heart failure itself has to be treated as well.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older man has a high BMI. Why can loss of muscle still be the problem that matters?
Sarcopenia is a muscle disorder, diagnosed on low strength and low muscle quantity, not on body weight, so
it can occur at a normal or high BMI (sarcopenic obesity when obesity is present). Loss of muscle is the
link in the malnutrition chain that causes weakness, falls and poor healing, so muscle has to be assessed
as well as weight.
:::

## Recognising and screening for malnutrition {#sec-mal-recognise}

### Who to suspect {#sec-mal-suspect}

Malnutrition is often silent, so recognising it starts with knowing whom to screen. Five groups carry
enough risk to warrant active screening [@bapenAtRisk; @fried2001frailty]:

- frail and pre-frail older adults in the community;
- people who are socially isolated, bereaved or living alone;
- the chronically ill, through the disease-related mechanism above;
- hospital inpatients;
- anyone in the post-discharge period.

Unintentional weight loss, or "shrinking", is a core feature of frailty (a clinical picture in older age
whose other features include weakness, slow walking and exhaustion; see the *Healthy ageing* chapter) and
one of the first things to ask about [@fried2001frailty]. Membership of an at-risk group raises the
pre-test probability (the chance, before any test, that the patient has the condition). You therefore
screen the patient instead of waiting for malnutrition to look obvious. Knowing the at-risk groups makes
malnutrition less likely to be missed.

### Nutrition screening: the generalist's role {#sec-mal-screening}

**Nutrition screening** is a fast, low-skill filter that anyone can apply to flag risk and trigger
referral, and it is the part of malnutrition care that falls to the generalist. It is deliberately not the
assessment, which the dietitian does. MUST (the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool, met in the
*Assessing diet and talking to patients* chapter) is a useful exemplar. It adds three components: a BMI
score, an unplanned weight-loss score, and an acute-disease effect (acutely ill and little or no intake for
more than about five days). The scores sum to an overall risk of low, medium or high, each tied to an
action, from routine re-screening to referral and a care plan [@bapenMUST].

Set each component in the screen below and watch the risk band and its action change.

<div data-island="must-screen" data-src="/diagrams/must-screen.yml"></div>

Weight loss and acute illness score independently of BMI, so a patient with a normal or even high BMI can
screen as high risk, and "she looks fine, her BMI isn't low" is the classic miss. Other tools suit other
settings, and all do the same job of flagging risk for referral:

- NRS-2002 (Nutritional Risk Screening 2002), for hospital inpatients [@kondrup2003nrs2002];
- the MNA-SF (Mini Nutritional Assessment short form), for older adults [@rubenstein2001mnasf;
  @kaiser2009mnasf];
- the WHO ICOPE (Integrated Care for Older People) vitality screen (two questions, on unintended weight
  loss and loss of appetite), in the community [@whoIcope];
- 3-MinNS (3-Minute Nutrition Screening), developed in Singapore [@lim2009minns].

::: {.callout-important}
## Screening is not diagnosis
A positive screen means *document, monitor and refer*; it is not a diagnosis and not a care plan. Formal
diagnosis applies the **GLIM criteria** (from the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) after a
positive screen. Malnutrition is diagnosed on at least one phenotypic criterion (weight loss, low BMI,
reduced muscle mass) plus at least one aetiological criterion (reduced intake or absorption, or
inflammation or disease burden): a phenotype of loss plus a cause [@cederholm2019glim; @jensen2019glim].
GLIM sits downstream of screening and is applied by the dietitian or team; the generalist's job is the
screen and the referral, not the diagnosis or the grading of its severity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can a patient with a normal BMI screen as high risk on MUST?
MUST adds three scores: BMI, unplanned weight loss and the acute-disease effect. The weight-loss score and
the acute-disease effect count independently of BMI, so recent weight loss, or an acute illness with little
or no intake for more than about five days, can put the patient in the high-risk band even when the BMI
scores nothing. That is why "her BMI isn't low" is the classic miss.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a nurse's screen comes back positive. Why is the patient not yet diagnosed with malnutrition, and what follows?
Screening is a fast filter that flags risk; it does not establish that malnutrition is present. Diagnosis
applies the GLIM criteria downstream (at least one phenotypic criterion, such as weight loss or reduced
muscle mass, plus at least one aetiological criterion, such as reduced intake or inflammation), and the
dietitian or team makes it. The positive screen's job is to trigger documentation, monitoring and referral.
:::

## Dietary management: nutrition support {#sec-mal-support}

### Oral nutrition support: a stepwise, food-first approach {#sec-mal-ons}

When intake is poor, oral nutrition support follows a stepwise approach (often drawn as a ladder), and the
first step is not a supplement:

1. Food-first, which fixes the cause of poor intake (isolation, poor dentition, low mood, dysphagia,
   finances or appetite-blunting drugs) and makes the most of ordinary meals.
2. **Food fortification**, which enriches familiar dishes so each mouthful carries more energy and protein
   without more volume (adding egg, minced fish, tofu, milk powder, oil or full-fat dairy) and can lift
   intake substantially [@bapenFoodFirst; @hpbSeniors].
3. **Oral nutritional supplements (ONS)**, the supplement drinks, which are an evidence-based add-on when
   food-based measures fall short, not the first step [@espenGeriatrics2019;
   @espenGeriatricsPractical2022].

**Enteral** (tube) and **parenteral** (intravenous) feeding are specialist steps beyond these, prescribed by
the team.

![Oral nutrition support is stepwise: start with food-first (fix the cause of poor intake and make the most of ordinary meals), then food fortification (more energy and protein per mouthful, no extra volume), then oral nutritional supplements as an add-on; enteral and parenteral feeding are specialist steps beyond these. The generalist screens, starts food-first and fortification, and refers; the plan itself is dietitian-led.](/figures/mechanisms/oral-support-ladder.svg){#fig-ons-ladder width="72%" fig-align="center"}

ONS are often started too early, and their benefit is modest. In at-risk older people ONS produce a
small, consistent weight gain and fewer complications, but no significant overall mortality benefit
[@milne2009ons]. Singapore's own SHIELD trial found that a specialised supplement improved a
composite of nutritional outcomes, but that result was driven by the weight component and came from an
add-on *to* dietary counselling, not a replacement for it [@shieldChew2021]. ONS are therefore a useful
tool, used after food-first and by a dietitian, but they do not fix malnutrition on their own.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out (and eating in)
Locally, food fortification means enriching familiar hawker and home dishes, since many older
Singaporeans eat soft, refined starch with too little protein. Add an egg, minced fish, tofu or extra
chicken to rice porridge; enrich *mee sua* or soup noodles with egg and protein toppings; choose
higher-protein *yong tau foo* items (fish paste, tofu, egg) over plain vegetables; reach for full-fat milk
and dairy. HPB's guidance for seniors rests on the same principles: nutrient density over quantity, more
protein, softer textures and more fluids [@hpbSeniors].
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do no harm: don't feed the starved patient up too fast
The instinct to "build them up quickly" is dangerous. In someone who has eaten little for a long time,
restarting feeding, especially carbohydrate, triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and
magnesium into cells, on top of thiamine depletion. The result is refeeding syndrome (see the
[*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-refeeding) chapter): a fall in blood phosphate
(hypophosphataemia) that can bring cardiac and neurological harm [@deSilva2020Refeeding;
@daSilva2020ASPEN]. The task here is to recognise the at-risk patient (very low BMI, large recent weight
loss, prolonged low intake, low baseline electrolytes, or a high-risk history such as alcohol or
chemotherapy) and **refer for cautious, monitored refeeding** [@niceCg32]. Managing it (the electrolyte and
thiamine replacement and the energy titration) is specialist, later learning.
:::

### Dysphagia and texture-modified food {#sec-mal-dysphagia}

Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing; see the *Healthy ageing* chapter) is a common, dangerous cause of
undernutrition, and it has recognisable red flags:

- coughing or choking on food or drink;
- a "wet", gurgly voice after swallowing;
- meals that drag on;
- recurrent chest infections;
- weight loss or dehydration.

The trap is to assume that no cough means a safe swallow. Up to a third of **aspiration** (food or drink
entering the airway) is silent, with no cough at all, so you refer on the pattern of red flags, not on the
cough alone [@wirth2016dysphagiaOlder]. The speech therapist assesses the swallow and sets the safe texture
level. Those levels share a standardised language, the **IDDSI** (International Dysphagia Diet
Standardisation Initiative) framework: a colour-coded scale from 0 to 7, so that "Level 4" means the same
thing in every ward and home [@cichero2017iddsi; @cichero2020iddsi2].

Texture-modified food improves swallow safety but tends to lower intake, because pureed and soft food delivers
less energy and calcium. It therefore needs fortifying and monitoring; a pureed diet does not solve the
problem on its own [@wu2020tmd; @espenGeriatricsPractical2022]. Singapore has adopted IDDSI as its
national standard through the MOH-led EatSafe SG programme, which spans hospitals, community hospitals,
nursing homes and social service agencies [@mohEatSafeSg; @iddsiSingapore].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older patient who is eating poorly is started on supplement drinks and nothing else. What should come first, and why?
Oral nutritional supplements are the third step, an add-on when food-based measures fall short. The
first step fixes the cause of poor intake (isolation, dentition, mood, dysphagia, finances or
drugs), and the second fortifies familiar dishes so that each mouthful carries more energy and protein
without more volume. The benefit of ONS is also modest: in at-risk older people they give a small,
consistent weight gain and fewer complications, but no significant overall mortality benefit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older patient started on pureed meals no longer coughs while eating. Why is the problem not necessarily solved?
Up to a third of aspiration is silent, so the absence of a cough does not prove a safe swallow; the
pattern of red flags (a wet voice, slow meals, recurrent chest infections) still matters. Pureed food also
tends to lower intake, because it delivers less energy and calcium, so it needs fortifying and monitoring.
:::

## When to refer {#sec-mal-team}

Nutrition support is a team activity, and each member has a distinct part [@sgPostDischarge2023;
@niceCG32NST]:

- the dietitian does the assessment and the plan;
- the doctor treats the underlying cause and champions nutrition by referring;
- the nurse screens and monitors intake;
- the speech therapist assesses swallowing and texture;
- physiotherapists and occupational therapists restore the function that lets improved eating last;
- the medical social worker addresses the social causes;
- the pharmacist watches drug–nutrient and electrolyte safety.

The doctor's distinctive contribution is the referral that sets the team in motion; the feeding plan is
the dietitian's. Nutrition is therefore best handled as interprofessional teamwork, not solo prescribing
[@aclm2022comp; @crowley2019] (see the *Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself* chapter).

::: {.callout-important}
## You screen and refer; you do not prescribe the feeding plan
The generalist screens (MUST or a local tool), recognises the at-risk patient and the red flags (weight
loss, poor intake, dysphagia, a social cause, refeeding risk), starts food-first and social support, and
refers to the dietitian and the team [@sgPostDischarge2023; @aclm2022comp]. The dietetic assessment and
GLIM diagnosis, the ONS and enteral prescriptions, refeeding management and IDDSI level-setting are all
team- and specialist-led.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older patient who lives alone screens high risk on MUST. What is the doctor's part, and what is left to the team?
The doctor recognises the at-risk patient and the red flags, starts food-first and social support, treats
the underlying cause and refers; that referral is what sets the team in motion. The dietitian then does
the assessment and the plan, the nurse monitors intake, and the medical social worker addresses social
causes such as living alone. The GLIM diagnosis, the ONS and enteral prescriptions, refeeding management
and IDDSI level-setting are all team- and specialist-led.
:::

## What does treating malnutrition look like for a generalist? {#sec-close}

It looks like catching malnutrition early and handing it on safely, without doing harm on the way: not
feeding a starved patient up too fast, and referring a risky swallow on its red flags instead of waiting
for a cough.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**Undernutrition begins in the community, not the ward.** In the population-based Singapore Longitudinal
Ageing Studies, more than 1 in 4 community-dwelling older adults (27.6%) were at malnutrition risk and nearly
half were pre-frail [@wei2017slasFrailty]. Malnutrition and frailty are related but distinct, and they
frequently co-occur. The harm concentrates where they co-occur: in the local cohort, poor nutrition combined with
pre-frailty or frailty carried the highest death rate and about 1.7 times the mortality risk after
adjustment, whereas poor nutrition alone showed no clear excess [@wei2018slasOutcomes]. The practical frame is to screen the frail senior for malnutrition specifically.
Nationally, about 1 in 4 adults aged 50 to 69 fall below minimum energy needs and about half below protein needs,
and standardised screening in polyclinics and Active Ageing Centres is under active discussion: a direction
of travel, not a settled mandate [@mohMalnutritionTracking2025; @mohPolyclinicScreening2026].

**Social eating is a practical target in Singapore.** In a local cohort, 24.1% of older adults ate alone most of the time
although only 6.7% lived alone (living *with* family is not the same as sharing a meal), and eating alone
tracks poorer diet quality and higher malnutrition risk [@ye2023daha; @wyman2025eatingAlone]. Loneliness,
more than objective isolation, predicts frailty locally [@geSocialFrailtySg2022], and one-person households
among seniors have more than doubled in a decade [@mohSeniorsAlone2026]. The question *"who do you eat
with?"* is therefore a nutrition question, and the answer often points to a social referral as much as a
dietetic one: communal dining and befriending through Age Well SG and the Active Ageing Centres
[@mohAgeWellSg2023; @aacSingapore2025].

**The hospital and post-discharge period is high-risk.** Among hospitalised older Singaporeans, about 35%
are malnourished at admission and about half by discharge, and malnutrition persists for weeks afterwards
[@sgPostDischarge2023]. The recommended model is to screen every patient early and let any clinician refer
directly to a dietitian, though local dietetic capacity is scarce, which is another reason to start
food-first and social support early. Singapore's own screening tool, 3-MinNS, was developed and validated
at the National University Hospital and can be administered by nurses [@lim2009minns;
@lim2013nurseScreening].
